column3: It closely repeats the objection that death, dust, and bones make subsequent judgment impossible.
Its return to Hell presumes the final outcome but does not address resurrection's possibility.
It directly states the sequence of life, death, and being brought forth from the earth.
It voices the same disbelief: death and dust are treated as making return implausible.
The claim that God has a son does not clarify the objection to resurrection.
Reviving the dead earth and bringing life from death explicitly grounds the promised human emergence.
It closely duplicates the skeptical question about being raised after becoming dust and bones.
Leaving darkness for light is a spiritual metaphor, not a relation to bodily resurrection.
God's giving life, causing death, then giving life again directly answers the focus question.
A human question at the upheaval of the earth only loosely echoes the focus's questioning form.
Jesus's blessed life and duties do not develop death followed by resurrection.
Its rhetorical question treats return after death as implausible, matching the focus's objection.
It repeats the denial of resurrection after death, dust, and bones almost verbatim.
The accusation against Moses does not concern death or renewed life.
The condemned acknowledge repeated death and life, overturning the assumption that death is final.
Decayed bones are presented as the material premise of the same denial of return.
The miraculous gift of a child broadly shows divine creative power but not resurrection itself.
The revival of dead earth is explicitly offered as proof that God revives the dead.
Human recollection on the Last Day presumes accountability but does not explain resurrection.
Moses's call to Pharaoh's purification has no useful connection to the focus.
God's sole power to cause death and life directly counters death as an autonomous final state.
The disbeliever's wish to be dust occurs at judgment but does not address being raised alive.
John's purity and compassion do not bear on the resurrection objection.
The earth holding the living and dead gives a limited setting for, not an answer to, resurrection.
God teaching humanity what it did not know only broadly contrasts with human disbelief.
A tree growing in Hell does not clarify human resurrection after death.
The ordinary emergence of the Prophet from rooms is unrelated to eschatological emergence.
God's creation of humanity broadly supports divine creative power without addressing renewed life.
Abraham's withdrawal from his people does not develop the focus's claim.
It directly asks who can revive decayed bones, the same material objection implied in the focus.
Spiritual aliveness in warning is distinct from being physically raised after death.
Elijah's challenge to idol worship does not clarify resurrection.
The demonstration of reviving dismembered birds directly answers how God revives the dead.
God's bringing forth pasture is only a remote creation analogy.
Ishmael's worship and divine approval do not concern death followed by life.
Life and death belonging to God frames both under one divine lordship, though it omits renewed life.
It closely parallels a son's rejection of the promise that he will be brought forth after death.
Almsgiving has no material relation to the focus.
The requested payment and barrier do not concern resurrection.
Bringing water and pasture from the earth is a remote sign of divine productive power.
Zechariah's emergence from the sanctuary is unrelated to the final emergence from death.
It explicitly argues that the Creator is able to give life to the dead.
Within the same surah, Jesus states that he will die and be raised alive, directly answering the focus.
It nearly reproduces the claim that people cannot be brought out after death, dust, and bones.
God causes a multitude to die and then restores them to life, a concrete counterexample to finality.
Mary's wish for death amid labor does not concern being raised after death.
Zechariah's failing bones provide only a physical echo of the focus.
God's power to give life and cause death challenges the view that death is beyond divine control.
The same surah explicitly joins birth, death, and being raised alive for John.
The contrast between believers and evildoers presumes judgment but does not explain resurrection.
Entering land after others leave is unrelated to being raised from death.
Demanding a sign from the Messenger does not develop the focus's denial.
The call to God with insight does not concern life after death.
God's ownership and power to give life and death supplies a theological basis for resurrection.
The surrounding punishment on the Last Day is only an indirect eschatological connection.
The emergence of daylight does not clarify human resurrection.
Abraham invokes God's power over life and death to refute a disbeliever's false claim.
Universal human mortality supplies the focus's premise but says nothing of being raised alive.
Joseph's preference for prison does not concern resurrection.
God as the Ever-Living is a broad theological basis, not a direct answer to the objection.
A demand for a sign is unrelated to death and renewed life.
Joseph's appearance before the women has no connection to resurrection.
Moses's shining hand is a miracle but does not illuminate life after death.
The ruined garden and its owner's regret do not address resurrection.
God's unrestricted power to create weakly supports resurrection but the verse concerns Christology.
Being brought forth as a community is not the emergence from death in the focus.
The first gathering and unexpected expulsion offer only a faint eschatological lexical association.
The plea to leave Hell follows judgment but does not clarify being raised from death.
Dying as Muslims concerns one's state at death, not life after it.
Provision brought out for earthly life does not address resurrection.
The word for payment is unrelated to the focus's being brought forth.
The conditional departure of groups does not concern resurrection.
The search for escape on the Last Day indirectly presumes the event after resurrection.
The incidental phrase about raising ranks has no relation to rising from death.
Dying in disbelief bears on final accountability but not the possibility of resurrection.
Iblis's expulsion is unrelated to the emergence of the dead.
The covenant's promise of gardens only broadly implies final recompense.
Abraham explicitly describes God as the one who will cause him to die and then give him life.
Iblis's expulsion does not clarify resurrection after human death.
Purifying the soul has no material relation to being raised alive.
The production of crops supports divine creative power only in a remote analogy.
The rebuke of human ingratitude broadly resembles the focus's unbelieving human speaker.
It places death as a stage in the human sequence, whose following verse proceeds to resurrection.
Mistaking worldly ease for honor does not concern life after death.
God's bringing living from dead and dead from living supports the power denied in the focus.
It repeats the same skeptical question about being raised after death, dust, and bones.
Desiring death as a test of claimed afterlife privilege is only tangentially related.
Lot's defense of his guests has no connection to resurrection.
The saved ask about no longer dying, which only indirectly contrasts with the focus's future resurrection.
Moses's admission of past error does not concern death or renewed life.
Human remembrance before Hell is an indirect consequence of the resurrection and judgment scene.
God's call brings people out of the earth, directly depicting the event doubted in the focus.
Rejecting the charge of soothsaying does not develop resurrection.
Fear of fighting like death has no useful relation to being raised after death.
The question about human semen begins a creation argument but alone does not establish resurrection.
God's knowledge of what leaves the earth is a broad, non-resurrection echo of emergence.
The question about cultivation is a remote creation analogy only.
Rain emerging from clouds is not an argument about resurrecting the dead in this verse.
Disbelievers questioning God's stated number faintly parallels the focus's skeptical questioning.
Iblis's commanded descent and expulsion do not clarify human resurrection.
It explicitly traces humanity from lifelessness to life, death, renewed life, and return to God.
God lets a man die for a hundred years and restores him to life, providing a concrete answer to the focus's doubt.
Bringing the living from the dead and the dead from the living supports the divine power denied in the focus.
Jesus revives the dead by God's permission, directly demonstrating divine authority over death.
God recalls Jesus's raising of the dead by His permission, a direct counterexample to death's finality.
It declares that God will raise the dead and return them to Him.
God takes souls in death-like sleep and raises people again until their appointed term, a limited analogy to renewed life.
God brings the living from the dead and the dead from the living, directly challenging a one-way view of death.
The revival of dead land by rain supplies a recurring natural sign of the renewal denied in the focus.
God begins creation and then repeats it, directly establishing return after death as part of His creative act.
The challenge asks who originates creation and then repeats it, directly refuting denial of renewed creation.
God gives life and causes death, and humanity returns to Him, grounding the focus's future emergence in divine rule.
It identifies disbelief in a new creation after becoming dust as the very objection at issue.
It directly rebuts the oath that God will not resurrect those who die, affirming His binding promise.
It repeats the question whether bones and scattered fragments can be raised as a new creation.
It records the objection asking who will restore the dead and answers: the One who created them first.
It states the denial of resurrection after becoming bones and fragments, then answers it by recalling first creation.
The Creator of the heavens and earth is declared able to create humans anew, directly answering the focus's inference.
The immediate next ayah refutes the speaker by recalling that God created him when he was nothing.
Humanity is created from earth, returned to it, and brought forth from it once more.
It challenges the claim that any earthly gods can raise the dead, affirming resurrection as a divine prerogative.
Every soul tastes death and returns to God, which frames death as a transition rather than the final horizon.
The folding of heaven is paired with repeating the first creation, a direct creation-and-recreation proof.
The detailed stages of human formation and reviving dead earth are given as proof of the Resurrection.
It explicitly states that God gives life to the dead and has power over all things.
It explicitly declares that the Hour is coming and that God will raise those in the graves.
It directly states that people will be raised on the Day of Resurrection after dying.
It voices the denial that, after living and dying, people will ever be resurrected.
It asks who begins creation and then repeats it, directly opposing the focus's denial.
It repeats the disbelief that people and their ancestors can be raised after becoming dust.
It preserves the same dust-and-ancestors objection as a recurrent form of denying resurrection.
It calls people to observe how God begins creation and then brings forth the later creation.
It commands reflection on creation's origin and God's bringing forth of the final creation.
Every soul's death and return to God form an indirect frame for the focus's postmortem question.
God begins creation, then repeats it, and people are returned to Him.
Repeating creation is declared easier in human terms for the One who originated it, directly answering the focus.
God creates, provides, causes death, and gives life, supplying the governing sequence behind resurrection.
Creating and resurrecting all humanity is described as no harder than creating or resurrecting one soul.
It records the objection that losing one's bodies in the earth could be followed by a new creation.
The angel of death takes people, after which they are returned to their Lord.
It quotes disbelief that complete disintegration could be followed by a new creation.
God revives dead land by wind and rain, then explicitly likens this to the Resurrection.
It directly declares that God gives life to the dead.
At the trumpet blast, people emerge from graves toward their Lord.
Those raised from their resting places ask who has resurrected them, directly mirroring the focus's issue.
The One who created bones the first time is declared able to revive them when decayed.
The Creator of the heavens and earth is affirmed able to create humans anew.
God's creative command is sufficient whenever He wills a thing, supplying the power behind resurrection.
The skeptics extend the same question to their forefathers' resurrection.
God takes souls at death and in sleep, showing that life and death remain under His direct control.
The trumpet blast is followed by people standing and looking on, directly depicting postmortem raising.
Creating the heavens and earth is presented as greater than creating people, refuting doubt about re-creation.
God gives life and causes death, and His command brings what He wills into being.
The One who revives dead land is explicitly declared the giver of life to the dead.
The revival of dead land is followed by the direct assurance: thus people will be brought forth.
It voices the claim that there is only the first death and no resurrection.
It records the claim that time alone destroys people and that there is no life beyond worldly death.
God gives life, causes death, and will gather humanity for the unquestionable Day of Resurrection.
The Creator of the heavens and earth is explicitly able to give life to the dead.
Rain revives dead land, followed by the direct statement that such is the emergence from graves.
People hear the blast from near, marking the moment they come forth from death.
The earth splits open over them as they emerge; this gathering is declared easy for God.
The second creation belongs to God, directly establishing re-creation after the first life.
People emerge from graves with lowered eyes at the call, directly portraying resurrection.
It repeats the question whether the dead and their forefathers will be raised.
The One who created humanity is invoked to confront refusal to affirm His creative power.
Knowledge of the first creation is presented as evidence that should prompt recognition of re-creation.
God gives life and causes death, providing a basic theological counterweight to death's finality.
The revival of dead earth is explicitly tied to God's power to give life to the dead.
God will resurrect all people and inform them of what they did.
It directly rebuts those who claim they will not be resurrected, affirming their resurrection and accountability.
God's creation of death and life places both conditions under His purposeful sovereignty.
People emerge swiftly from graves at the summons, directly depicting the event denied in the focus.
God returns people to the earth and will bring them forth from it again.
It challenges the assumption that God will not gather a person's bones.
It affirms God's ability to reassemble even the smallest details of a human body.
After death and burial, God will resurrect the human when He wills.
It rebukes those who fail to realize that they will be raised for a tremendous Day.
The Creator is declared able to return the human, a concise proof of restoration after death.
